title: The World Cup Starts in Two Weeks. India Still Has No Broadcaster. A DC-Based NRI Firm Says It Won the Bid.
excerpt: FIFA wanted $100 million. Reliance offered $20 million. Sony walked away. Now Zee, Prasar Bharati, and an Indian American LLC are all scrambling for the rights.
body:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off on June 11 in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. It will feature 48 teams for the first time. Broadcasters in more than 180 countries have signed deals. India — the world's most populous country, with a fast-growing football audience — is not one of them.

With 14 days until the opening match, India's 1.4 billion people have no confirmed way to watch the World Cup on television or streaming. The situation is, by any measure, extraordinary.

## The Price Gap That Broke Everything

FIFA initially sought $100 million for the combined broadcast rights to the 2026 and 2030 World Cups in India. The number was ambitious — India accounted for just 2.9% of the global linear TV reach of the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

The Reliance-Disney joint venture (JioHotstar), India's dominant sports streaming platform, offered $20 million. FIFA held firm at no less than $60 million. The talks deadlocked.

Sony, which could have been a natural buyer, evaluated the rights and decided not to bid at all. The gap between what FIFA wanted and what the Indian market would pay was simply too wide. FIFA eventually revised its expectations down to roughly $35 million. Still no taker.

## Enter Zee — and an NRI Firm From Washington

On May 26, Zee Entertainment announced it was in active talks with FIFA to broadcast the World Cup in India. The company disclosed the discussions as part of its launch of Unite8 Sports, a new portfolio of sports channels. No financial details were shared.

But there is another claimant. Avni LLC, an Indian American investment firm based in Washington, DC, says it submitted a corporate guarantee backed by financial commitments exceeding $300 million in February 2026 as part of FIFA's closed tender process. The firm claims an associated partner secured the winning bid after competing against several major Indian broadcasters.

"The Indian subcontinent alone has the ability to exceed initial valuation expectations," said Deelip Mhaske, President and CEO of Avni LLC. The firm is pitching a vision beyond traditional television — OTT platforms, AI-powered multilingual broadcasting, mobile micro-subscriptions, and esports integrations across Asia.

FIFA has declined to confirm or deny either claim, saying only that discussions "are ongoing and must remain confidential at this stage."

## The Courts Get Involved

The situation has become urgent enough for legal intervention. The Delhi High Court has issued notices to the Centre and Prasar Bharati following a petition seeking mandatory free-to-air broadcast on DD Sports to prevent a total blackout.

Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav heard the writ petition filed by advocate Avdhesh Bairwa, which argues that depriving millions of football fans from watching one of the world's biggest sporting events would violate public interest principles.

India's public broadcaster Prasar Bharati is reportedly the last bidder still formally engaged with FIFA, raising the possibility that the World Cup could air on Doordarshan — free-to-air, but with limited streaming infrastructure for the diaspora.

## What This Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora in the US, UK, and Canada, the broadcast chaos at home is frustrating but not directly disabling — they can watch on their local broadcasters. But the absence of an Indian broadcast deal means no Hindi, Tamil, or Bengali commentary, no Indian studio shows, no shared viewing experience across WhatsApp groups with family back home.

It also means a missed commercial moment. India's football audience has been growing rapidly, driven by the ISL and Premier League viewership. A World Cup without an Indian broadcaster is a setback for the sport's momentum in the country.

The contrast with other markets is stark. China's state broadcaster CMG sealed its deal with FIFA on May 15. Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka all have arrangements. India stands alone among major cricket-and-football nations without a confirmed deal.

## What Happens Next

The most likely scenario is a last-minute deal with either Zee or Prasar Bharati — possibly a hybrid arrangement where DD Sports provides free-to-air coverage while a private partner handles streaming. SSEN, another contender, has bid a modest $2 million for the rights, pitching itself as a free-streaming option across South Asia.

But "last minute" is running out fast. The opening match between Mexico and the host United States is 14 days away.

For now, India's football fans do what they have been doing for months: they wait.
